presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset severe headache with left-sided weakness and vomiting while gardening, followed by progressive decline in consciousness over 30 minutes.
history: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension (self-reported non-adherence to amlodipine) developed abrupt severe headache and left-arm weakness at 4pm while gardening in hot weather. He vomited twice within minutes of onset. Family noted he became increasingly drowsy and slurred in speech over the next 20-30 minutes before collapsing. No witnessed seizure. No head trauma. No fever preceding the event. He is a known hypertensive for 12 years, intermittently on treatment, with no known diabetes, no prior stroke or TIA, no anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and no history of alcohol excess or bleeding disorder. No recent illness or infective symptoms.
examination: Drowsy, opens eyes to voice, localizes to pain on the right but only withdraws on the left (GCS 10: E3V2M5). Left hemiparesis (upper limb 1/5, lower limb 2/5) with left facial droop and left-sided sensory neglect. Right gaze preference. Pupils 3mm equal and reactive bilaterally at presentation. Plantar response extensor on the left. Neck supple, no meningism. Cardiovascular exam: markedly elevated blood pressure, regular rhythm, no murmurs. No signs of endocarditis or embolic phenomena. No skin rash, no petechiae.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head: acute hyperdense hematoma in the right basal ganglia/thalamus, approximately 35 mL by ABC/2, with mild surrounding edema and 4mm midline shift; intraventricular extension into the right lateral ventricle; no evidence of underlying mass, aneurysm, or arteriovenous malformation on initial review
CT angiogram head: no spot sign identified; no aneurysm or vascular malformation seen
differentialDiagnoses: Ruptured cerebral aneurysm with intraparenchymal extension
Haemorrhage from underlying arteriovenous malformation or cavernoma
finalDiagnosis: Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage (basal ganglia/thalamic ICH with intraventricular extension)
citations: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage 2022
contraindications: Avoid antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents in the acute phase
Avoid aggressive/rapid overcorrection of blood pressure below systolic 140 mmHg due to risk of cerebral hypoperfusion
Avoid thrombolytics and mechanical thrombectomy (contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke)
Avoid hypotonic IV fluids (risk of worsening cerebral edema)
edgeCases: Deep basal ganglia/thalamic location with classic hypertensive history strongly favors hypertensive etiology, but CTA should be reviewed for underlying vascular lesion, especially if patient is younger or hematoma is lobar
Intraventricular extension increases risk of obstructive hydrocephalus requiring neurosurgical consultation and possible external ventricular drain
If INR/coagulopathy or antithrombotic use were present, urgent reversal would take priority over BP control
Deterioration in GCS or pupillary asymmetry should prompt urgent repeat CT to assess for hematoma expansion or hydrocephalus
This diagnosis (ich) is present in the diagnosable disease list under Neurology/Vascular
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag this as a hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage (deep/basal ganglia location) requiring urgent BP control (target SBP ~140 mmHg), neurosurgical/ICU consultation for intraventricular extension, and explicit avoidance of antithrombotic/thrombolytic therapy.

Repeat CT head if clinical deterioration
